FAR Wing Aspect Ratio

Wing aspect ratio in FAR

FAR gives each wing panel a lift slope from its effective aspect ratio. Upstream FAR estimates that panel by panel, so the same wing lifts differently depending on how it was cut into parts. This PR (branch fix/spanwise-aspect-ratio) measures the whole wing each panel belongs to, tip to tip, through the fuselage between the roots.

  • The lift no longer depends on how a wing is cut: the Hera’s wing as one panel or four gives the same lift slope (3.34 per radian both ways, where upstream gives 2.20 and 1.49), and B9 rebuilds of stock planes lift within −11 to +3% of the stock parts (upstream −36 to +54%).
  • Against a vortex lattice on eight real aircraft, the median lift-slope error falls from 30% to 1% (real aircraft).
  • On eight NACA wind-tunnel wings, the aspect ratio FAR uses goes from 1.40 to 1.01 times the geometric one, and the median lift-slope error from +19% to +11% (measured wings).
  • Upstream’s aspect ratios change from one load of a craft to the next; this PR’s repeat within 1%.
  • The stock planes still fly: the cruise trim angle moves by under half a degree on most (stock planes, in flight, transonic and supersonic).

Known gaps (details): the XB-70A’s neutral point lands 0.11 chord ahead of the wind tunnel’s; the B-2 lifts 13% above the lattice; winglets get too much credit; FAR has no tail downwash. Opt-out: a switch in FAR’s Model Options window restores upstream exactly (opting out).

Upstream is drawn in orange and this PR in green throughout. A percentage given as an error is a difference from a measurement or from the lattice: the smaller its size, above or below 0%, the better.

The wing, two ways

One side of the RSP-432 Hera Jet, rebuilt with streamwise joints, drawn from the part outlines KSP exports. The outline is the original's; following its corners takes a few narrow panels at the strake and the tip, shaded but not labeled. Wide panels are labeled with their area and semispan b/2. Grey panels get no lift from FAR in either layout: its voxels count them as shielded by the fuselage. Above them, the craft as it sits in the SPH, at the same scale.

Upstream FAR panel by panel

Each panel uses its own semispan over its own chord, then multiplies by a factor FAR calls ARFactor. FAR finds it by casting five rays sideways from mid-span: a panel with something at one end gets ×2 (the root), and one with something at both ends gets up to ×8, a stand-in for a panel in the middle of a longer wing. FAR never measures how much longer that wing is, and what the rays hit varies from one load of a craft to the next (the Gull’s mean aspect ratio from 6.4 to 7.6 over nine flights).

AReff = (b/2 ÷ c)panel × ARFactor    main panel: 0.80 × 4.40 = 3.54    one segment: 0.23 × 6.80 = 1.55

Aspect Ratio per Panel

The rays find a neighbor at both ends of the main panel and of each segment, so both get a large factor. But a segment's own aspect ratio is a quarter of the main panel's, so cutting the panel into four cuts its aspect ratio about fourfold, and the whole craft’s lift slope drops by a third (2.20 to 1.49 per radian).

This PR per wing

This PR groups the panels into wings and gives every panel its wing’s aspect ratio:

  • One wing: panels of the same kind that touch, in about the same plane, however the wing was cut: along the span, along the chord, or overlapping. Touching is judged on the parts’ models as the player sees them; a bend where two panels meet (dihedral) still joins them, a layer stacked above another does not.
  • Control surfaces join the wing they touch, directly or through another control surface (a flap behind a spoiler), and count in its area. Each is measured by its model’s outline at rest, so one on a swept hinge keeps its streamwise side edges.
  • Left out: panels FAR counts as shielded. A panel that touches no other, such as one on an engine nacelle, keeps upstream’s value.
  • The root picks the formula. A wing that spans the centerline is measured whole. A wing whose root sits on a bare fuselage, with nothing lifting between the roots (the Hera’s case), is measured as the whole wing through the body: its span from tip to tip, the strip of body between the roots in its area (the strip follows the wing’s inboard edge, so engines beside the fuselage count), and the whole wing’s half-chord sweep; its panels carry the strip’s lift. Any other covered root, such as one against another wing, doubles the half wing’s aspect ratio, as ARFactor does.
  • A covered tip (a winglet or a pod) counts as an endplate, worth up to a quarter more; the Hera’s winglets close its tips.
AReff = b² ÷ 2 (S + Sstrip) × (1 + ¼ ftip) (root on a bare body)    b: span from tip to tip, through the body    S: one side’s planform area, control surfaces included, overlaps counted once    Sstrip: the strip of body from that root to the centerline    ftip: the share of the tip that is covered, 0 to 1    main panel, either layout: 3.44

Aspect Ratio per Panel

upstreamthis PR shading: effective aspect ratio, 0 to 4 (same scale in every drawing)

What FAR does with it

With this PR both layouts give the same aspect ratio and lift slope. It also raises the one-panel layout’s lift slope by half (2.20 to 3.34 per radian) although its main panel’s aspect ratio barely moves (3.54 to 3.44): the small panels at the strake and the tip, which upstream gives aspect ratios down to 0.25, now take the wing’s 3.44, and the strip of body between the roots is in the wing’s area and carries lift. The next section shows why that strip belongs.

  2. The elevon is layout dependent upstream too: FAR finds the wing ahead of it with a single ray from its root, so with the main section in four segments it sees one segment instead of the main panel. With this PR it hangs from the whole wing in either layout and takes its aspect ratio. ↩︎

Lift carried across the body

A fuselage between two wing roots carries the wing’s lift across: slender-body theory has the wing and the body together lift as the whole wing would through the body, and the body raises the lift on the wing beside it. Upstream FAR has part of that: a root its rays find covered by the fuselage doubles the panel’s aspect ratio, so the panel lifts as half of a wing mirrored at the fuselage’s side, the two exposed halves joined at the root. The body between the roots is left out: its width from the span, and the lift it carries.

Two NACA wind-tunnel models of wings on bodies measure the lift of the whole combination. Beside them, a vortex lattice: a potential-flow solution of the same planform, from the parts’ outlines as KSP exports them (the far-vlm tool, which also exports FAR’s own numbers). The lattice solves each model three ways: with the body between the roots bridged by a flat plate at the root chord; the wing panels alone, the gap left open; and the two exposed halves moved in to meet at the centerline, which is what upstream’s covered root amounts to.

ModelBody width / spanMachMeasuredLattice, wing + plate Lattice, wing panelsLattice, exposed halves joined
RM A53C20, AR 2 pointed wing0.170.242.292.34 +2%1.811.61
RM A53C20, AR 2 pointed wing0.170.502.232.42 +8%1.881.67
RM L54B03, 60 deg delta0.140.092.302.43 +5%1.961.78

Lift slope per radian on the reports’ reference areas (RM A53C20, a pointed wing of aspect ratio 2; RM L54B03, a 60° delta); the percentage is the lattice’s error from the measurement. Inviscid theory runs a few percent above a real wing; the body’s own nose adds about 0.08 more.

The lattice with the body bridged matches the measured total. The exposed halves joined fall 23–30% short of it: the strip of body between the roots lifts, and it lifts the wing beside it 10–12% more. FAR’s fuselage does not make that up: its body model lifts a fuselage from the change of its cross-section along its length, as slender-body theory lifts a nose, not as a strip of wing; on the real aircraft below it leaves the joined wing 11–35% short (appendix). So this PR puts the strip in the wing. Whether the wing then lifts right is the next question: the next four sections check it against wind-tunnel wings, the XB-70’s tunnel model, and the lattice on eight real aircraft.

Measured wings

Wind-tunnel wings, checked directly. NACA TN 3497 (Dods & Tinling, 1955) measured seven tapered tails of one area, aspect ratio 3 to 6 and up to 45° of sweep, each with a 30%-chord elevator; TN 2080 an untapered aspect ratio 3.13 panel with 25%-chord flaps. Each is rebuilt in KSP as one B9 wing panel a side ahead of the hinge, with B9 control surfaces behind it, on a 0.3 m body. FAR’s lift slope in the editor (Mach 0.2) against the measured one:

FAR’s lift slope in the editor (Mach 0.2) on eight wind-tunnel wings rebuilt in KSP, against the slope the report measured, with the aspect ratio each build gives the wing; the percentages are FAR’s errors. The median row takes each column’s middle value over the eight wings, the aspect ratios as a multiple of each wing’s geometric one (nearer 1× is better).

What remains with this PR, +11% at the median, is FAR’s lift formula, which runs above these tests even at the right aspect ratio: this PR lands on each wing’s geometric aspect ratio, measuring the panel and its control surfaces as one wing through the body. Upstream gives each about 1.4 times it: the panel ahead of the hinge is only 70% of the chord, so its own semispan over chord is too large, and the elevator strip gets its own from its narrow chord.

The reports’ own figures beside the rebuilds: each model as the report draws it and as it is built in KSP (wing panel blue, elevator or flap dark orange, a fixed strip pale), and its measured lift curves at each deflection beside FAR’s on the same axes: upstream dashed, this PR solid, the measured lift slope dotted through zero. FAR’s curves start at −4°, where the runs did. Only the undeflected curves, drawn bold, test the aspect ratio: their slope is the lift slope in the table above, to set against the dotted measured one. The faint deflected curves show FAR’s flap model, which this PR leaves alone (appendix). Scans from NTRS: TN 3497, TN 2080; select a figure for full size.

XB-70A against the wind tunnel

NASA TP-1514 (Daugherty, 1979) tested a 0.03-scale XB-70-1 at Ames from Mach 0.6 to 2.53, with the canard on and off. The aircraft is rebuilt from the report’s model tables (the wing, the canard and the twin fins; the propulsion nacelle under the wing) on a fuselage traced from the USAF three-view, the canard at the station NASA CR-2011-217078 gives for the airplane, its canard all-moving and its fins too, as the airplane’s were. FAR’s numbers are from the editor, on the report’s reference area (6,298 ft²) and mean chord (78.5 ft), moments about its quarter-chord; the measured ones are read off the report’s figures with its wing tips undeflected. The neutral point is in mean chords behind the chord’s leading edge. Subsonic, this PR’s lift slope lands within 8% of the tunnel’s, where upstream’s is 28 to 30% low; but this PR puts the neutral point about 0.11 chord ahead of the tunnel’s.

At Mach 1.4 both builds are close. The neutral point goes the other way from the lift slope: upstream sits on the tunnel’s subsonically, within 0.01 chord with the canard on and off, and this PR about 0.11 chord ahead of it. The canard’s own share (the shift between on and off, 0.075 chord in the tunnel) is about right on both builds (0.08), so it is the wing’s aerodynamic center that this PR moves forward. Supersonic, the tunnel’s neutral point moves aft to 0.38 chord with the canard; neither build follows it (0.20 to 0.26). Both builds give no lift at zero angle of attack, where the model has a little negative lift (−0.02 to −0.05).

Real aircraft, in game

Eight real aircraft built in KSP from published three-views, each wing cut into convex B9 panels where its outline bends, with its trailing-edge control surfaces as separate parts (build details). The lattice solves each wing (or tail) alone with the fuselage between its roots bridged by a flat plate at the root chord, and counts the lift on the wing and on the plate: the lift the wing makes with its body, as the body section shows. FAR’s numbers are its own in game, the lift on the wing’s parts, control surfaces included. This PR lands within 5% of the lattice on 8 of the 10 surfaces, a median error of 1% against upstream’s 30%; its largest miss is the Northrop B-2, +13%.

FAR’s lift formula on the whole wing

With a wing on a bare body measured whole, FAR’s lift formula (Helmbold’s, as in DATCOM) gets the whole wing’s aspect ratio and half-chord sweep. On the real aircraft it lands within 2% of the lattice’s wing and plate on six of the eight; it is 5% above on the Cessna and 13% on the B-2:

The stock planes

The 14 stock planes that ship with KSP and FAR, and a KerbalX build of the de Havilland Vampire, in FAR’s editor at Mach 0.5. Lift slopes change by −16% to +42%. Where upstream overrated a wing’s aspect ratio (the Firehound, the Gull, the Ravenspear Mk3, the SkyEye, the Vampire) the center of lift moves forward and the static margin shrinks. Each drawing marks the center of mass and the center of lift: the neutral point, where the lift added as the angle of attack rises acts, from FAR’s own pitching moment; the other build’s center of lift is dashed. The further the center of lift sits behind the center of mass, the more nose-up elevator the plane needs to hold a given lift: the table sets the most lift full nose-up input can hold against the lift cruise needs.

FAR editor simulation at Mach 0.5. Lift slope per radian from 0° to 4°, on FAR’s reference area; the change is this PR against upstream, neither better nor worse in itself. Static margin: the center of lift’s distance behind the center of mass over FAR’s reference mean aerodynamic chord (MAC); over 100% (the SkyEye, the Vampire, the Stearwing) the center of lift sits more than a chord behind. Trim CL: the lift coefficient where the pitching moment at full nose-up input crosses zero, along the AoA fit (* only past 60°, far beyond the stall: no practical limit). Cruise needs the weight over dynamic pressure at 3 km and Mach 0.48 (10.3 kPa). Red: full nose-up falls more than 10% short of cruise; amber: within 10% of it. “No limit”: the center of lift is at or ahead of the center of mass.

Stearwing A300 lift slope 3.87 → 5.48 (+42%), static margin 230% → 251%

Panel AR: upstream 12.1, this PR 7.9. The CoL moves 0.50 m aft: static margin 230% → 251% of the MAC. Full nose-up input trims CL 0.14 → 0.21 (at 6° → 6°); cruise at 3 km and Mach 0.48 needs 0.21. Not enough pitch authority to hold cruise upstream. Cruise needs about all the nose-up input there is with this PR. In flight it rolls into a spiral dive and hits the sea on every build.

Thunderbird lift slope 2.98 → 3.34 (+12%), static margin -1% → 12%

Panel AR: upstream 1.4 to 8.0, this PR 3.4. The CoL moves 0.21 m aft: static margin -1% → 12% of the MAC. The CoL sits at or ahead of the CoM (no static margin), so there is no nose-up trim limit; the autopilot holds it.

shading: effective aspect ratio, 0 to 16 (the Hera drawings use 0 to 4). Control surfaces are grey; panels FAR counts as shielded by the fuselage are pale grey. Quartered circle and dark line: center of mass; blue circle, arrow and line: center of lift; dashed blue line: the other build’s center of lift.

In flight

The stock planes flown in steady cruise at 3 km and Mach 0.5 on AtmosphereAutopilot (an autopilot mod that trims and holds altitude and speed), once on upstream FAR and once with this PR, and shot with FAR’s aerodynamic visualization on. Every plane that holds the cruise upstream holds it with this PR; the trim angle moves by under half a degree on most, and the lift-to-drag ratio moves both ways. Each part is tinted by its lift coefficient (cyan; a wing saturates at Cl 0.25, a body at 0.05), and FAR’s own force arrows show each part’s lift (cyan) and drag (red), their lengths to scale with the force. Both builds hold the same altitude and speed, so the total lift is the plane’s weight in both; what changes is how much angle of attack and elevator it takes, and how the lift is shared between the parts. The FAR SkyEye flies autostrutted with its flaps up, and is shown at Mach 0.8 as well; the Ravenspear Mk4 crashed at Mach 0.5 on upstream, so it is shown at Mach 0.8 instead; the Stearwing A300 rolls into a spiral dive on both builds. The XB-70A is the wind-tunnel rebuild, flown in the RP-1 Minimal install (sources).

Cruise numbers: angle of attack (* not steady within 2 minutes), pitch input (−1 to 1), lift over drag, the lift slope from FAR’s prediction at the flown state (per radian on the wing area, so not the stock table’s, which is the editor’s on FAR’s reference area), and the wing parts’ effective aspect ratio, area-weighted. Upstream’s aspect ratios come from sideways raycasts and change from one load to the next (the Gull from 6.4 to 7.6 over nine runs); this PR’s repeat within 1%.

Transonic and supersonic

The supersonic-capable planes flown in cruise at 7 km and Mach 0.95, then climbing to a cruise at 12 km and Mach 1.5, once on upstream FAR and once with this PR, on the same autopilot. FAR’s lift between Mach 0.9 and 1.4 is a blend of its subsonic and supersonic models, and its supersonic lift scales with the aspect ratio through the leading-edge factor, so this PR changes both regimes. At Mach 1.5 the trim angle moves by at most 0.2° and the lift-to-drag ratio by at most 5% (the Dove) on the planes that hold the cruise. Near Mach 0.95 the changes follow the subsonic ones: the Aeris 4A and the Ravenspear Mk4 trim at less angle and fly more efficiently, the Firehound MS at less angle and about the same lift-to-drag ratio, the Dove, the Mirage and the Ravenspear Mk3 at more.

Opting out

This PR comes with a switch: whole-wing aspect ratio, in FAR’s Model Options window (right-click FAR’s toolbar button, in the editor or in flight). Switched off, every wing panel keeps its own aspect ratio, as upstream FAR has it. On the eight real aircraft at Mach 0.3, 0.5 and 0.8, off reproduces upstream FAR’s own build and on reproduces this PR’s, every lift slope to three decimals and no part’s aspect ratio moved (appendix). The real aircraft and the XB-70A above come from this one build, switched off for upstream and on for this PR.

Known limitations

  • The XB-70A’s neutral point. Subsonic, this PR puts it about 0.11 chord ahead of the wind tunnel’s, where upstream sits on it; supersonic, neither build follows the tunnel’s aft shift, and at Mach 1.2 this PR’s lift slope is 24% low (XB-70A).
  • The Northrop B-2 lifts 13% above the lattice: FAR’s lift formula runs about 10% high on this planform, with or without a body (lift formula).
  • Winglets get too much credit: a covered tip raises the 737 wing’s aspect ratio to 11.2, against 9.45 traced and about 10.4 by Hoerner’s rule for a winglet’s height; at 9.45 FAR’s formula gives 4% less lift. That is for a separate change.
  • No tail downwash: the wing’s downwash cuts the lift of both real tails by about 38% in the lattice, and FAR has no model of it, in the editor or in flight. That is for another change.
  • FAR’s lift formula runs above the NACA tests even at the right aspect ratio: +11% at the median (measured wings).
  • A panel that touches no other keeps upstream’s raycast value: the Ravenspear Mk3’s outer delta on its nacelle, which leaves its B9 twin 11% off the stock plane.
  • Pitch authority: with this PR the Ravenspear Mk3’s full nose-up input trims CL 0.23 in the editor, against 0.44 for cruise, though it holds the cruise in flight; the Ravenspear Mk4 and the Stearwing A300 are short of elevator on both builds.
  • Stowed spoilers: FAR’s editor simulation counts shielded control surfaces that flight leaves out (the 737’s spoiler plates, 5% of its wing’s lift): a FAR bug, fixed in a separate change.

Appendix: methods and notes

Where the numbers come from

Editor numbers are FAR’s editor simulation; flights are flown on AtmosphereAutopilot. The real aircraft and the XB-70A come from the one build that carries the switch, every real aircraft exported in one KSP start with the switch off and again with it on; every export records the switch as the exporter read it back. The stock planes are measured with this PR as it stood with three fixes found flying them: the strip of body between the wing roots follows the wing’s inboard edge, so engines beside the fuselage count; overlapping panels lift once over the area they share; the wing’s center is the fuselage, not an engine beside it. The KX Vampire is a KerbalX RO build of the de Havilland Vampire (about 0.58 scale, 6.75 m span, its wing on a 1.1 m pod), not a faithful rendition, so it is with the stock planes, not the real aircraft. The XB-70A and the Concorde fly in the RP-1 Minimal install, a second KSP install with RP-1, whose upstream FAR is a different build from the stock planes’. The 737’s craft lists each engine first among the parts hung from its wing root: which of two touching parts FAR gives a voxel cell they share depends on the order it takes them in, and with the engines listed last the 0.4 m strip of wing under each engine pylon came out shielded and made no lift.

Building the real aircraft

Six come from one template, on a procedural fuselage of the real width; the Cessna’s tailplane sits 0.46 m below its wing (the drawing’s front view). The 737 is a flyable build of its own, traced from the drawing’s side, top and front views: a procedural fuselage, the wing with its dihedral and winglets, landing gear and engines, and the control surfaces measured off the drawing’s lines: an inboard and an outboard flap, an aileron, and two spoilers a side, each a thin plate laid into the wing’s top surface ahead of its flap (the flight spoilers as one panel, and the ground spoiler), the wing whole beneath them, elevators from the root to 6.55 m on a tailplane 1.4 m above the wing, and a rudder 1.3 m deep at its root; the leading-edge slats stay part of the wing, as FAR has no model of them. The Concorde is a flyable build of its own too: a fuselage traced from the drawing’s side and top views (61.7 m, flat underneath), its wing 0.82 m below the fuselage axis and drooping toward the tips as the drawing’s front view has it (0.9 m at the tip, the panels each tilted to meet at their joints), elevons, fin and rudder, landing gear and engines; it flies and takes off in game. The lattice takes each panel’s height from its own surface, so the Concorde’s drooped panels meet at their joints as the wing’s do. The 737’s is solved flat: its 7.5° dihedral moves a lift slope by about 2 %, and its spoilers, thin plates on its top surface, are left to the wing beneath them, in the lattice, in the wing’s area and in FAR’s lift: stowed, they are shielded and FAR gives them no force in flight.

The percentages are the lift missing against the lattice’s wing on the body. Lift per radian (m², lift over dynamic pressure), at the real aircraft table’s Mach. The lattice solves the wing alone, its control surfaces included: on the body, with the body between its roots bridged by a plate at the root chord; joined, with its two exposed halves moved in to meet at the centerline. FAR’s fuselage lift is the whole craft’s less its wing and tail parts’, from AoA 0 to 4° in the editor with the switch off; it is the same model in flight. Even counted whole, nose and all, it leaves the joined wing 11–35% short. Upstream FAR in game falls further short on most of these (the real aircraft table): its covered root helps only the panels at the root, and each panel keeps its own aspect ratio. The 737’s lattice is solved flat, as there.

FAR’s flap model

The same wings with their flaps deflected test FAR’s flap model, which this PR leaves alone: FAR turns the flap strip to the deflection, which gives about 60% of the measured lift at small deflections (TN 3497, TN 2080, Report 554), too much at 30–40°, and a stall past about 45° where measured plain flaps keep gaining to 60°. Upstream and this PR differ there only because FAR lifts the deflected strip with that strip’s lift slope.

The XB-70A’s canard and its earlier flights

The canard is from NASA CR-2011-217078’s table II (the airplane’s own data, as in TP-1514): 28.8 ft span, 20.8 and 8.06 ft chords, 31.7° leading edge, its quarter-chord mean chord 37.7 ft ahead of the wing’s. The USAF three-view the fuselage is traced from draws the canard’s leading edge at about 49°, against its own labels, and its tip 6.7 ft too far aft; the craft first took the canard’s station from that tip, and the wind-tunnel table is from the craft with it moved forward. That moves the neutral point with the canard on 0.006–0.008 chord forward on both builds and leaves the lift slopes as they were.

The XB-70A was reflown after the canard moved 2 m forward, which changes the trim angle by under 0.1° on either build. The rest of the change from the earlier flights (upstream 4.88°, this PR 2.91°; L/D 8.8 and 12.1) is the install’s intakes, which FAR now gives their scaled size: their ram drag goes from 9 to 46 kN, and the lighter intakes take more elevon to trim.
